encouragement.high: You nailed it. You can look at a fraction and just see how big it is now — that is a real skill, go show someone!
encouragement.mid: Nice work. You already know how to split a whole into equal parts, and the ones you missed are the next thing you get to learn.
encouragement.low: You tried every single question, and that is exactly how this starts. Fractions click all at once — let's go again.

slides.narration: Imagine a big pizza cut into eight equal slices. Every slice is exactly the same size, so each one is one eighth of the whole pizza.
slides.caption: A pizza cut into 8 equal slices
slides.imagePrompt: A whole round pizza cut into eight equal slices on a red checkered tablecloth, seen from directly above, warm and inviting

slides.narration: Now you eat two slices. Six are still sitting there. Six out of eight slices left is the same amount as three quarters of the pizza.
slides.caption: 2 eaten, 6 still on the tray
slides.imagePrompt: The same round pizza from above with two slices missing, leaving a gap, the remaining slices still arranged in a circle on a red checkered tablecloth

quiz.prompt: You ate 2 of the 8 slices. What percent of the pizza is left?
quiz.explanation: Six of the eight slices are left. Six eighths is the same as three quarters, and three quarters is 75%.

slides.narration: Here is the tricky part about fractions. A bigger bottom number means the pieces are smaller, because you cut the same thing into more parts.
slides.caption: Bigger bottom, smaller pieces
slides.imagePrompt: Two identical chocolate bars side by side on a wooden table, the left one broken into three big chunks and the right one broken into eight small chunks

slides.narration: So one third is actually bigger than one eighth. Three is a smaller number than eight, but the piece it makes is bigger.
slides.caption: One third beats one eighth
slides.imagePrompt: A child's hand holding one large chunk of chocolate next to another hand holding one tiny chunk, on a wooden table, friendly and clear

quiz.prompt: Which piece of chocolate is the biggest?
quiz.explanation: One third is biggest. Cutting the bar into only three parts leaves each part larger than cutting it into four or eight.

slides.narration: A habitat is just the place where an animal already has everything it needs. Food, water, shelter, and space to move around.
slides.caption: A habitat is a home that provides
slides.imagePrompt: A sunlit forest clearing with a stream, a hollow log, berry bushes and a deer standing among the trees, storybook illustration

slides.narration: That is why a polar bear would not last in a desert, and a camel would not last on the ice. Each one is built for its own home.
slides.caption: Built for their own home
slides.imagePrompt: A split scene: a polar bear on blue ice under falling snow on the left, and a camel on golden sand dunes under a bright sun on the right

quiz.prompt: Which of these does an animal need from its habitat? Pick all of them.
quiz.explanation: Food, shelter and water are what a habitat has to provide. A name is something people give an animal, not something it needs to survive.

slides.narration: Inside every habitat, energy moves along in one direction. The sun feeds the plants, the plants feed the animals that eat plants.
slides.caption: Energy travels in one direction
slides.imagePrompt: A bright meadow with the sun above, tall green grass, and a rabbit nibbling at the grass, cheerful storybook illustration

slides.narration: And then a hunting animal eats that one. Follow the chain backwards from any animal and you always end up back at the sun.
slides.caption: Follow it back to the sun
slides.imagePrompt: A fox crouched in tall meadow grass watching a rabbit in the distance, warm afternoon light, storybook illustration

quiz.prompt: Tap these in order to build the food chain, starting with where the energy comes from.
quiz.explanation: The sun feeds the grass, the grass feeds the rabbit, and the rabbit feeds the fox. Every food chain starts at the sun.
